title: The prophets did not borrow from Plato
source_text: Πολλὰ δ᾿ ἂν καὶ παρὰ τῷ Μωϋσεῖ εὑρεθείη καὶ τοῖς προφήταις, οὐ μόνον Πλάτωνος ἀλλὰ καὶ Ὁμήρου καὶ τῆς τῶν παρ᾿ Ἕλλησι γραμμάτων εὑρέσεως πρεσβυτέροις, ἄξια τῆς εἰς αὐτοὺς χάριτος τοῦ θεοῦ καὶ μεγαλονοίας πεπληρωμένα· οἵτινες οὐχ, ὡς οἴεται Κέλσος, παρακούσαντες τοῦ Πλάτωνος τοιαῦτ᾿ εἰρήκασι. πῶς γὰρ οἷόν τ᾿ ἦν τοῦ μηδέπω γενομένου αὐτοὺς ἀκηκοέναι; ἵνα δὲ καὶ ἐπὶ τοὺς Ἰησοῦ ἀποστόλους τις, νεωτέρους γενομένους Πλάτωνος, ἀναγάγῃ τὸν Κέλσου λόγον, ὅρα εἰ μὴ αὐτόθεν ἀπίθανόν ἐστι τὸ λέγειν Παῦλον τὸν σκηνοποιὸν καὶ Πέτρον τὸν ἁλιέα καὶ Ἰωάννην τὸν καταλιπόντα τὰ δίκτυα τοῦ πατρὸς, παρακούσαντας τῶν Πλάτωνι ἐν ταῖς ἐπιστολαῖς εἰρημένων, τοιαῦτα περὶ τοῦ θεοῦ παραδεδωκέναι. πολλάκις δὲ ἤδη ὁ Κέλσος θρυλήσας ὡς ἀξιούμενον εὐθέως πιστεύειν, ὡς καινόν τι παρὰ τὰ πρότερον εἰρημένα πάλιν αὐτό φησιν· ἀρκεῖ δ᾿ ἡμῖν τὰ εἰς ταῦτα λελεγμένα. ἐπεὶ δὲ καὶ ἄλλην λέξιν ἐκτίθεται Πλάτωνος δι᾿ ὧν φησιν, „ἐρωτήσεσι καὶ ἀποκρίσεσι χρωμένων“ ἐλλάμπειν φρόνησιν τοῖς κατ᾿ αὐτὸν φιλοσοφοῦσι, φέρε παραδείξωμεν ἀπὸ τῶν ἱερῶν γραμμάτων ὅτι προτρέπει καὶ ὁ θεῖος λόγος ἡμᾶς ἐπὶ διαλεκτικὴν, ὅπου μὲν Σολομῶντος λέγοντος· „παιδεία δὲ ἀνεξέλεγκτος πλανᾶται,“ ὅπου δὲ τοῦ τὸ σύγγραμμα τὴν Σοφίαν ἡμῖν καταλιπόντος Ἰησοῦ υἱοῦ Σιρὰχ φάσκοντος· „γνῶσις ἀσυνέτου ἀδιεξέταστοι λόγοι.“ εὐμενεῖς οὖν ἔλεγχοι παρ᾿ ἡμῖν εἰσι μᾶλλον. τοῖς μαθοῦσιν ὅτι δεῖ τὸν προϊστάμενον τοῦ λόγου δυνατὸν εἶναι „τοὺς ἀντιλέγοντας ἐλέγχειν.“ εἰ δὲ ῥᾳθυμοῦσί τινες, οὐκ ἀσκοῦντες προσέχειν ταῖς θείαις ἀναγνώσεσι καὶ ἐρευνᾶν „τὰς γραφὰς“ καὶ κατὰ τὴν ἐντολὴν τοῦ Ἰησοῦ ζητεῖν τὴν διάνοιαν τῶν γραφῶν καὶ αἰτεῖν περὶ αὐτῶν ἀπὸ τοῦ θεοῦ καὶ κρούειν αὐτῶν τὰ κεκλεισμένα, οὐ παρὰ τοῦτο ὁ λόγος κενός ἐστι σοφίας.
pass_a_gloss: Many things would be found also in Moses (Μωϋσῆς) and the prophets (προφῆται), older not only than Plato but also than Homer and the invention (εὕρεσις) of letters (γράμματα) among Greeks, worthy (ἄξια) of the grace (χάρις) of God toward them and filled (πληρόω) with greatness-of-mind (μεγαλόνοια); who not, as Celsus thinks (οἴομαι), having misheard (παρακούω) Plato said such things. For how possible to have heard one not yet born (γίνομαι)? And that someone may carry back (ἀνάγω) Celsus's argument (λόγος) also to Jesus's apostles, become younger than Plato, see whether it is not on its face (αὐτόθεν) unpersuasive (ἀπίθανος) to say that Paul the tentmaker (σκηνοποιός), Peter the fisherman (ἁλιεύς), John who left (καταλείπω) the nets (δίκτυα) of his father, having misheard things said by Plato in the letters (ἐπιστολαί), handed down (παραδίδωμι) such things about God. Often already Celsus having harped (θρυλέω) that [one is] required (ἀξιόω) to believe (πιστεύω) at once (εὐθέως), as something new (καινός) beyond things said before says it again; enough for us what was said to these. Since he sets out (ἐκτίθημι) another phrase (λέξις) of Plato by which he says, 'of those using questions (ἐρώτησις) and answers (ἀπόκρισις)', wisdom (φρόνησις) shines in (ἐλλάμπω) those philosophizing after him, come let us show from the sacred writings that the divine word (θεῖος λόγος) too urges (προτρέπω) us to dialectic (διαλεκτική), where Solomon says 'instruction (παιδεία) unrefuted wanders (πλανάω)', where Jesus son of Sirach who left us the treatise (σύγγραμμα) Wisdom (Σοφία) says 'knowledge (γνῶσις) of the senseless (ἀσύνετος): unexamined words'. So kindly (εὐμενής) refutations (ἔλεγχοι) are rather among us, those who learned that the one presiding (προΐσταμαι) over the word must be able 'to refute (ἐλέγχω) those speaking against (ἀντιλέγω)'. If some are lazy (ῥᾳθυμέω), not practising (ἀσκέω) attending to divine readings (ἀναγνώσεις) and searching (ἐρευνάω) 'the Scriptures' and according to Jesus's command (ἐντολή) seeking (ζητέω) the sense (διάνοια) of the Scriptures and asking (αἰτέω) God about them and knocking (κρούω) at their closed things (κεκλεισμένα), not because of this is the word empty (κενός) of wisdom (σοφία).
pass_b_english: Many things could also be found in Moses and the prophets, who are older not only than Plato but even than Homer and than the invention of letters among the Greeks, things worthy of the grace God gave them and filled with greatness of mind. These men did not, as Celsus supposes, say such things because they had misheard Plato. For how could they have heard a man who had not yet been born?

And even if someone applies Celsus’s argument to the apostles of Jesus, who lived later than Plato, consider whether it is not unbelievable on the face of it to say that Paul the tentmaker (Acts 18:3), Peter the fisherman (Matthew 4:18), and John, who left his father’s nets (Matthew 4:21–22), handed down such teaching about God because they had misheard what Plato said in his letters.

Celsus has already harped many times on the charge that people are required to believe at once, and now he says it again as if it were something new beside what he said before. What we have said in answer to this is enough for us.

Since he also sets out another passage of Plato, in which he says that wisdom shines out upon those who practise philosophy in Plato’s way “when they use questions and answers” (Plato, Seventh Letter 344b), come, let us show from the sacred writings that the divine word also urges us toward dialectic. In one place Solomon says, “Instruction left unexamined goes astray” (Proverbs 10:17); in another Jesus son of Sirach, who left us the book called Wisdom, says, “The knowledge of the senseless man is unexamined talk” (Sirach 21:18). So it is rather among us that kindly refutations are found, among those who have learned that the one who presides over the word must be able “to refute those who contradict” (Titus 1:9).

But if some are careless, and do not train themselves to attend to the divine readings, to “search the Scriptures” (John 5:39), and, as Jesus commanded, to seek the meaning of the Scriptures, to ask God about them, and to knock at what is shut in them (Matthew 7:7), the word is not for that reason empty of wisdom.

choices.choice: Celsus’s charge (6.1) is that Christians took their ideas from Plato and ‘misheard’ (παρακούσαντες) him; kept as ‘misheard’. ἵνα ... ἀναγάγῃ is concessive (‘even if someone applies’). ‘When they use questions and answers’ is Plato, Seventh Letter 344b (ἐρωτήσεσιν καὶ ἀποκρίσεσιν χρωμένων), which Celsus quoted; the rest of the clause is Celsus’s paraphrase (Plato’s ἐξέλαμψε φρόνησις becomes ἐλλάμπειν φρόνησιν), and ‘he says’ is Celsus, since κατ᾿ αὐτόν means ‘in Plato’s way’. ‘Kindly refutations’ (εὐμενεῖς ἔλεγχοι) picks up Plato’s own words in the same passage (ἐν εὐμενέσιν ἐλέγχοις); left unquoted because the edition does not mark it. θεῖος λόγος here is the teaching of Scripture, which Origen then quotes, so ‘the divine word’ is lowercase, as is ‘the word’ at the end of the chapter (the Christian teaching). The edition puts a full stop after μᾶλλον, but the dative τοῖς μαθοῦσιν goes with παρ᾿ ἡμῖν and is translated as one sentence. Proverbs 10:17 is quoted in the LXX form, which differs from the Hebrew-based English. Sirach 21:18 matches the LXX wording; Origen calls the book ‘Wisdom’ and its author ‘Jesus son of Sirach’ (Ben Sira’s Greek name). The ask/seek/knock allusion is Matthew 7:7 (also Luke 11:9). ‘Attend to the divine readings’ may echo 1 Timothy 4:13 (πρόσεχε τῇ ἀναγνώσει), a possible allusion only, not cited inline. Titus 1:9 τοὺς ἀντιλέγοντας ἐλέγχειν is rendered ‘to refute those who contradict’, with no object supplied. The tentmaker, fisherman and nets details are allusions, cited beside each name.
ἵνα ... ἀναγάγῃ: 'wants to turn ... against' changed to concessive 'even if someone applies ... to'
restored the ἐπεί subordination ('Since he also sets out ..., come, let us show')
added inline source (Plato, Seventh Letter 344b) for the quoted Platonic phrase
θεῖος λόγος lowercased to 'the divine word' (Scripture's teaching, not the divine Person)
Proverbs 10:17: removed doubled 'goes ... goes' ('Instruction left unexamined goes astray')
Sirach 21:18: ἀδιεξέταστοι λόγοι 'words that will not bear examination' (modal shift) corrected to 'unexamined talk'; ἀσυνέτου singular kept
εὐμενεῖς ... μᾶλλον reworded to natural order ('So it is rather among us that kindly refutations are found')
Titus 1:9: removed the supplied object 'it' ('those who contradict')
notes updated (1 Timothy 4:13 possible echo; speaker of the Plato paraphrase)
